passage:
I had promised Ms. Reyes four dozen oatmeal cookies for our class bake sale on Saturday, so bringing them was my job. Grandma Bea left her recipe card on the counter and asked if I wanted help, but I told her I could do the work myself.

The card said to use softened butter, but the butter had set hard in the refrigerator, and waiting for it would take an hour. To save time, I melted it in the microwave, which seemed like a clever shortcut. The first tray came out as one flat, greasy sheet. It was a mistake, and it was far from perfect.

Grandma watched from the doorway without a word. A few minutes later Ana came over with the sign she had painted for our table. 'You can still save it,' she said. 'Break it into pieces and call them oat crisps. They might sell even better.' I shook my head at the ruined tray. 'That skips fixing what went wrong,' I said. 'It just gives the mistake a new name.'

The rest of the dough was as runny as soup, so I scraped it into the trash and started a new batch, waiting this time for the butter to soften. Grandma came in once, tapped the words softened butter on the card, and went to bed. I had tried to save an hour, and it was past eleven when the last tray came out.

On Saturday the buyers emptied our table by ten. Ms. Reyes took a bite, raised her eyebrows, and said, 'Whoever baked these took their time.' I laughed, because she had no idea how much, and that night I printed two words across the top of the recipe card: SOFTENED BUTTER.

passage:
For forty years, the only way across the Marrow River at Pellam Ford was a wooden raft pulled along a steel cable. Children from the west bank rode it to school, and the ferry was how Otto Brandt, the ferryman, made his living.

In the fall of 1956, a teacher named Ida Venn asked the town council for a footbridge. Most people liked the idea, but the town had no money for it. So Ida's students began fundraising. They sold apples and washed cars, and by Christmas they had raised ninety dollars.

That winter, Ida counted crossings at the landing and found more than three hundred a week. Some had called the bridge a waste, guessing that only a few families used the ferry, and the count proved them wrong. Otto said her count included the same riders twice. He saw a bridge as a threat to his living, and he asked his riders to withdraw their support. A careful pilot, he said, kept the ferry safe even in high water. He warned friends the council would give in sooner or later.

In April, high water closed the ferry for nine days, and children missed school. At the next meeting, members agreed the crossing was risky for children. Then they voted the bridge down again because of its cost. The ferryman went back to his cable as soon as the river fell, his mind unchanged.

The students kept going. In March 1958 they handed the council $1,400, enough for the lumber and steel. With the cost paid, members approved the bridge that same night. It opened in October, and Otto, after one last trip across, sold his raft for firewood.

passage:
For forty years, the only way across the Marrow River at Pellam Ford was a wooden raft pulled along a steel cable. Children from the west bank rode it to school, and the ferry was how Otto Brandt, the ferryman, made his living.

In the fall of 1956, at a town council meeting, a teacher named Ida Venn raised the idea of a footbridge. Most people in town had ridden with Otto since childhood and saw the bridge as a threat to the ferryman's living.

That winter Ida counted crossings at the landing and found more than three hundred a week, far more than a few families. Her students began fundraising and soon had enough money for the railings. The count showed the bridge would be no waste, yet members kept putting off a vote; Otto's feelings worried them more than the cost. Otto had run the ferry safely in high water for forty years.

In April, high water reached the landing steps, and Otto tried one crossing with three children aboard. Halfway over, the cable slipped, and the raft swung toward the rapids before it caught. Everyone reached shore, shaking. That night Otto told his wife that the ferry had become too risky to run in high water, and that he had changed his mind about the bridge.

The council, which had seen high water every few springs, made no change after the flood. Then, at the May meeting, Otto stood up and gave the bridge his support. He told them that his living mattered less than the children's safety. Members trusted the man who knew the river best and approved the bridge that night. It opened in October 1957, and Otto walked across it first.

passage:
For forty years, the only way across the Marrow River at Pellam Ford was a wooden raft pulled along a steel cable. Children from the west bank rode it to school, and the ferry was how Otto Brandt, the ferryman, made his living.

In the fall of 1956, a teacher named Ida Venn asked the town council for a footbridge. Most people in town guessed that only a few families still crossed the river, and a bridge seemed a waste of money. Each morning Otto raised the ferry's gate, and Ida's class filed aboard with a handful of farmers.

The students began fundraising anyway. Bake sales brought in sixty dollars, a small part of the cost. Otto gave neither side his support. He saw little risk in high water; when the river rose, he simply tied up and waited until it was safe. Some wondered whether a bridge would be a threat to the ferryman's living, but Otto told Ida the council would come around in time.

In April, high water closed the ferry for a week. On the second morning, Ida saw a crowd waiting on the far bank: mill workers, a mail carrier, children, a doctor with his bag. She realized the town's guess was wrong. When the ferry reopened, she and her students began counting crossings from dawn to dark.

In one week they counted 412 crossings, more than the council had guessed for a month. Otto checked the figures against his fare book and said they were right. Faced with the numbers, members changed their minds, and the vote in May approved the bridge. It opened in October 1957, and Otto made one last trip across, waving to the crowd.

passage:
For forty years, the only way across the Marrow River at Pellam Ford was a wooden raft pulled along a steel cable. Children from the west bank rode it to school, and the ferry was how Otto Brandt, the ferryman, made his living.

In the fall of 1956, a teacher named Ida Venn asked the town council for a footbridge. Most people in town thought the ferry was safe enough, and the council set the idea aside. Certain the council would vote the bridge down for good, Otto raised his fare from five cents to a dime that winter.

That winter Ida counted crossings at the landing and found more than three hundred a week, far more than a few families. Her students began fundraising, too, and their bake sales brought in some money toward the cost. Members praised both efforts but gave the bridge little support, calling it a waste while the ferry ran well. Some called it a threat to the ferryman's living. Otto laughed at talk of risk. It was the safest crossing on the river, he said.

In April, high water tore the ferry loose from its cable while Otto carried four riders, two of them children. The raft spun half a mile downstream before farmers caught it with ropes near the mill. No one was hurt. The ferryman's mind was unchanged, and he promised to have the ferry running again by summer.

The council met two days later. Members who had called the ferry safe now spoke of the children on the spinning raft, and they approved the bridge before the meeting ended. Nobody mentioned the cost. It opened in October 1957, and Otto took a job painting its railings.
